2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`.    - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low concern: Administrative data cover a complete balanced sample of all 152 target municipal local governments (si and gun) in each of the three analyzed cross-sections (2010, 2016, and 2021; Obs = 152 across Tables 5 and 8-15) with no missing observations.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: While regressions control for binary private consignment and local public enterprise status alongside administrative unit (si/gun), financial independence, and per-capita local tax burden, critical confounders are omitted—most notably municipal population size/density (which mechanically enters the Coulter benchmark Ei and correlates strongly with si/gun status and fiscal independence), mountainous terrain, water source proximity, resident income, and unobserved time-invariant municipal heterogeneity across the three waves.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate for basic administrative classification, weak for institutional depth: Statutory/administrative categories—si vs gun administrative status, local public enterprise special-account status (Local Public Enterprises Act special account vs general account), private operational consignment to K-water, fiscal independence ratio, and per-capita local tax burden—are accurately sourced from official government portals (MOIS, NEC, NSO, ME), but coded only as coarse binary or aggregate variables without municipal tariff ordinance structures, block rates, or consignment contract duration/targets.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Although underlying water utility inputs come from official Ministry of Environment Water Supply Statistics, applying Coulter's extensive population-share allocation formula (Xi/S - Ei) to intensive rate and unit-price variables (average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, and water supply rate) severely distorts municipal inequity measurement by making scores largely a mechanical function of population share Ei (as partially acknowledged in Footnote 14). Additionally, customer satisfaction is proxied solely by raw complaint counts, penalizing municipalities with lower-than-expected per-capita complaints as inequitable.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: High concern (weak construct validity of composite outcome despite reliable raw administrative data): Raw municipal indicators (average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, water supply coverage rate, staff count, and complaint count) are drawn from standardized national Water Supply Statistics (ME, 2023), but transforming intensive prices and percentages through Coulter's population-share index yields implausible equity benchmarks (e.g., a theoretical unit price of 5,734 won/m3 for a populous city in Section 4.1) and conflates low complaint volume with distributional inequity.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported (No information). Full regression tables for all six dependent variables across all three years (Tables 9-14) and OLS robustness checks (Appendix Table 15) are reported, and the author candidly notes limitations regarding Coulter unit-price interpretation (Footnote 14) and Tobit non-censoring (Section 4.2). However, municipality-level adjustment tables omit five indicators and part of the sample due to space limits (Footnote 12), several municipalities are anonymized, Table 3 contains formula/translation errors, Table 5 has a population SD typo (250,34), and Tables 12 and 13 display identical LR chi-square, Pseudo R2, and Log likelihood values across all three years.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Low concern within the defined municipal target universe: The study includes all 152 city and county (si/gun) local water supply operators out of 161 nationwide after explicitly excluding 9 special/metropolitan cities and special self-governing provinces. Excluding metropolitan utilities is substantively reasonable given structural scale differences, though it limits generalizability to Korea's largest urban water systems.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are explicitly defined: from all 161 local water supply operators nationwide in South Korea, special/metropolitan cities and special self-governing provinces were excluded, yielding all 152 basic local governments (si and gun) observed in 2010, 2016, and 2021 based on data availability.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The institutional setting of Korean municipal water utilities, differences between urban cities (si) and rural counties (gun), K-water consignment arrangements, local public enterprise special accounts, and descriptive statistics (mean, SD, min, max for N = 152 in 2021) for all service and explanatory variables are clearly presented.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Explanatory political, regional, fiscal, and operational variables (mayoral re-election status, si/gun administrative unit, financial independence ratio, log per-capita local tax burden, private consignment status, and local public enterprise status) are measured using standardized official registries (NEC, Statistics Korea/Public Data Portal, Ministry of Environment, and MOIS Cleaneye), although binary operational indicators do not capture contract duration or tariff ordinance nuances.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Standardized statutory and administrative definitions from official Korean national databases (Ministry of Environment Water Supply Statistics, MOIS local public enterprise disclosures, and National Election Commission records) were applied uniformly across all 152 local governments.

Operational control variables (private consignment and local public enterprise status) were explicitly identified from prior literature, alongside regional (si/gun) and fiscal covariates. However, major structural and geographical confounders acknowledged elsewhere in the narrative—particularly municipal population size/density (which enters the Coulter outcome formula directly), mountainous terrain, water source availability, and resident income—were omitted from the analytical model.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.3 (PDF pp. 4-5, Tables 2 & 4), Section 4.1 (PDF p. 6), Section 5 (PDF p. 13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Although multivariable Tobit and OLS regressions included binary operational controls, no analytical strategy addressed mechanical scale confounding by population size/density (embedded in the Coulter benchmark Ei and correlated with si/gun status and financial independence), geographical/topographical differences, or unobserved time-invariant municipal heterogeneity across the three waves (no panel fixed/random effects).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2.2 & 3.3 (PDF pp. 4-5), Section 4.2 (PDF pp. 9-12, Tables 9-14), Appendix Table 15 (PDF p. 15)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: While raw utility metrics come from official Water Supply Statistics, the analyzed dependent variable (municipal Coulter inequity share) suffers from major construct validity flaws: (1) four of six indicators (average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, and water supply coverage rate) are intensive rates/unit prices rather than extensive quantities, so comparing Xi/S against population share Ei treats prices proportional to municipal population as the equity ideal—generating implausible theoretical prices such as 5,734 won/m3 (Section 4.1, Footnote 14) and making municipal scores largely reflect population share Ei; and (2) customer satisfaction is measured solely via raw complaint counts, where squared deviations treat fewer-than-expected complaints per capita as inequity. Table 3 also misstates the population ratio formula as its reciprocal.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2.1 & 3.3 (PDF pp. 3-5, Eq. 1-2, Table 3), Section 4.1 (PDF pp. 7-9, Table 7, Footnote 14)

domain_ratings.justification: Multiple statistical issues undermine inference: (1) separate cross-sectional regressions were run for 2010, 2016, and 2021 (Obs = 152 each) rather than longitudinal panel models accounting for repeated municipal observations and clustered errors; (2) Eq. 1 defines an aggregate national scalar I, whereas Tables 9-14 regress municipal-level inequity contributions that are heavily driven by population share Ei without controlling for population, explaining why slope estimates in Tables 9-13 are nearly identical across distinct water indicators; (3) as acknowledged in Section 4.2, dependent values were uncensored, rendering Tobit redundant with OLS (Table 15); and (4) Tables 12 and 13 report identical LR chi-square, Pseudo R2, and Log likelihood values across all three years, indicating a tabulation error.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2.1-3.2.2 (PDF pp. 3-4), Section 4.2 (PDF pp. 9-12, Tables 9-14), Appendix Table 15 (PDF p. 15)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High methodological concern under the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies. Strengths of Ko (2024) include complete administrative coverage of all 152 city and county (si/gun) local water supply utilities in South Korea across three time points (2010, 2016, and 2021), reliance on standardized official national datasets (Ministry of Environment Water Supply Statistics, MOIS, NEC, and Statistics Korea), transparent reporting of OLS robustness checks alongside Tobit estimates, and candid acknowledgment of analytical limitations in Footnote 14 and Section 4.2. However, severe construct validity and econometric limitations compromise the empirical findings. Most critically, four of the six service outcomes (average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, and water supply rate) are intensive ratios or unit prices rather than extensive divisible totals; inserting them into Coulter's population-share inequity formula (Xi/S - Ei) treats municipal water rates or unit prices proportional to population share as the benchmark of equity, yielding implausible theoretical unit prices (e.g., 5,734 won/m3 for a populous city) and causing municipal inequity scores to be mechanically dominated by population share Ei. Similarly, operationalizing customer satisfaction via raw complaint counts treats lower-than-expected complaints per capita as inequitable. In the second-stage regressions, estimating separate cross-sectional models for each year without panel fixed effects, clustered standard errors, or controls for population size/density and terrain leaves estimates heavily confounded by municipal scale—reflected in nearly identical regression coefficients across substantively distinct water indicators in Tables 9-13—and Tables 12 and 13 exhibit duplicated model-fit statistics.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Repeated cross-sectional observational municipal-level regression study (Coulter distributional inequity index calculation and separate cross-sectional Tobit and OLS regressions for 152 South Korean local governments in 2010, 2016, and 2021)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract & Korean Summary (PDF p. 1); Section 3.1-3.3 Research Model, Coulter & Tobit Equations, Sample & Variables, Tables 1-4, Footnotes 1-11 (PDF pp. 2-5); Section 4.1 Equity Level Analysis, Tables 5-7, Footnotes 12-14 (PDF pp. 6-9); Section 4.2 Tobit Regression Analysis, Tables 8-14, Footnote 15 (PDF pp. 9-12); Section 5 Conclusion (PDF pp. 12-13); Appendix Table 15 & Footnote 16 (PDF p. 15).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is a quantitative observational study analyzing secondary administrative records for 152 municipal water utilities in three separate cross-sections (2010, 2016, and 2021) via cross-sectional Tobit and OLS regressions examining political, regional, fiscal, and operational correlates of distributional inequity scores. Because no specific intervention or policy change is evaluated with a quasi-experimental or comparative longitudinal counterfactual design (ruling out ROBINS-I) and no incident cohort follow-up of initially outcome-free units is conducted (ruling out JBI Cohort), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
